svg.title: Payment Platform Target Architecture v2 — five services
svg.text: Five request-serving services + one worker · one session writer · one queue · one poster
All five deployed on every server
queue → LMS (rate limited) · sweeper · reconciliation by status API
no ingress · the ONLY caller of LMS posting
Session and agreement are SIGNED, not carried.
A token from another session or agreement fails the
signature. Binding is cryptographic, not a lookup.
One token per session · reusable · dies with it
Session 5 min sliding. Replaces single-use with
ECDH unchanged — the key never rides in the token
Downstream reads session:key to decrypt. One read.
Callbacks and status polling need NO session.
1 · Scheduler on every server → SKIP LOCKED claim
2 · Two posting writers → one queue, one poster
4 · LMS timeout then retry → unique client reference
Sources 1, 2 and 4 occur on a single server too.
More servers made them frequent, not possible.
Zero rows updated is never an error — it means
someone else already won. Ack and move on.
Gateway status API by tvstxnid, driven by next_check_at
Same total window as a fixed 30-minute cycle, but the
common case resolves in minutes — and it makes FEWER
vendor calls, because most resolve on the first check.
The terminal state is the point.
A bounded retry window with no terminal state means
payments silently vanish from tracking. UNRESOLVED
alerts and lands on an operator's desk with the tvstxnid,
the gateway, and every status response received.
1 · Is LMS posting idempotent on a client reference?
decides whether duplicate source 4 is closed
2 · Hard LMS rate ceiling, or a request to be gentle?
3 · Partner agreement fetch — scoped or unscoped?
4 · Partner notifies, or initiates money movement?
6 · LMS concurrency ceiling → bulkheads + server count
7 · Cloud or on-prem, for the network spec
Five deployables at ~10 req/sec is real operational
cost. Worth it if release cadences differ per service.
Build order: shared library → posting queue + constraints → claim-and-transition primitives (tested against real Oracle) → services

Gateway callback signature verification is the single highest-value control. The legacy verifyGatewaySignature returned true and its result was ignored — a forgeable payment success reachable by anyone who can guess a transaction id.
